statement: Each of the four edges of a square is painted either black or white. Two paintings count as the same if one can be rotated onto the other. How many genuinely different paintings are there?

choices.misconception: I counted every colouring of the four edges and forgot that rotations make some of them identical.
I divided 16 by 4, but that only works when no painting is left unchanged by a rotation, and some are.
I halved 16, treating only the 180 degree turn as a symmetry.
I listed by how many edges are black but forgot that two black edges can be adjacent or opposite.

hints: Some paintings survive a turn unchanged.
Group the paintings by how many edges are black: 0, 1, 2, 3 or 4.
Zero black: 1 way. One black: 1. Two black: 2 (adjacent or opposite). Three black: 1. Four black: 1. Total 1+1+2+1+1 = 6.

solutions.reliable: Divide-by-four fails here, because some paintings are unchanged by a rotation, so classify by hand instead. Group by the number of black edges. All white: 1 painting. Exactly one black edge: any single edge can be rotated to any other, so 1. Exactly two black: the two black edges are either adjacent or opposite, and rotation cannot turn one into the other, so 2. Exactly three black: 1, by the same argument as one. All black: 1. The total is 1 + 1 + 2 + 1 + 1 = 6. The transferable idea: when symmetry is involved, case-splitting on an invariant feature - here the number of black edges - is safer than dividing.
solutions.elegant: The count of black edges survives any rotation, so classify by it and only the two-black case splits, into adjacent and opposite.

whyOnTest: Dividing by the number of symmetries is the standard trap, and it is wrong exactly when some object is fixed by a symmetry.
author: Devansh Sanghavi
